title: What 81,000 people told us about the economics of AI
author: Maxim Massenkoff · Saffron Huang

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core distinction between meaningful but uneven task-level gains and broader, unproven organisational or labour effects. It materially extends the synthesis with large-scale worker-reported evidence showing occupational and career-stage variation, including relatively mild gains in legal professions and greater displacement concern among early-career workers and occupations with higher observed Claude exposure. Its self-selected sample, inferred measures and correlational design reinforce the cluster’s caution against treating reported productivity or exposure as causal evidence of realised value or job loss.
qs: The two groups exhibiting the mildest productivity improvements were workers in scientific and legal professions.

For about half of respondents in this survey, we were able to infer career stage from their answers.2 We found that early-career respondents were much more likely to express concern about job displacement than senior workers.

st.t: Junior hiring: Stable unemployment can hide adjustment
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by showing that reported productivity gains can coexist with displacement anxiety, especially among early-career workers, and by noting fears that junior positions may be replaced. It appropriately treats these findings as self-reported and correlational rather than evidence of actual displacement or net job loss.
qs: For about half of respondents in this survey, we were able to infer career stage from their answers.2 We found that early-career respondents were much more likely to express concern about job displacement than senior workers.

Some worried about this in the abstract: one software developer cautioned about “the possibility of AI in its current state being used to replace junior positions.” Others lamented that their jobs, or aspects of their jobs, were being automated away.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious account of substantial perceived productivity gains coexisting with concentrated early-career displacement anxiety, while treating exposure and concern as correlational rather than evidence of realised job loss. It does not directly examine legal workflows, verification or competence formation, so its support is strongest for the cluster’s productivity and labour-market claims.
qs: We learned that many people fear job displacement—though they also feel more productive and empowered at work.

For about half of respondents in this survey, we were able to infer career stage from their answers.2 We found that early-career respondents were much more likely to express concern about job displacement than senior workers.

st.t: Observed use: Capability predictions exceed workplace adoption
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between reported AI benefits and demonstrated workplace or employment transformation. It finds substantial self-reported productivity gains alongside displacement anxiety, but treats these as exploratory perceptions from a self-selected survey rather than evidence of actual job loss; comparatively mild gains in legal work also reinforce the cluster’s sector-specific caution.
qs: The mean productivity rating was 5.1, corresponding to “substantially more productive.” Our respondents were, of course, active Claude users who were willing to take a survey.

Relatedly, because the survey is open-ended, our measures are based on what respondents happen to mention; these findings should be confirmed in structured surveys that ask about these topics directly.

kp.k: Survey findings reflect self-selected users and inferred attributes
kp.d: In their April 22, 2026 report, Maxim Massenkoff and Saffron Huang analyse a survey described as covering 81,000 Claude users; the acknowledgements specify 80,508 participants. Claude-powered classifiers infer occupations, career stages, sentiments and productivity effects from open-ended responses. The authors caution that personal-account users who chose to respond are not representative, contextual inferences can be wrong, and spontaneous mentions should be tested through structured surveys.
qs: We thank the 80,508 Claude users who shared their stories.
Throughout this report, we use Claude-powered classifiers to infer people’s attributes and sentiments from their responses.
First, our survey is limited to users of personal accounts on Claude.ai who chose to respond.

Relatedly, because the survey is open-ended, our measures are based on what respondents happen to mention; these findings should be confirmed in structured surveys that ask about these topics directly.

kp.k: Observed AI exposure correlates with perceived displacement threat
kp.d: One fifth of respondents voiced economic-displacement concerns. Occupational observed exposure measures the percentage of job tasks for which Claude is used, rather than realised job losses. A 10-percentage-point exposure increase was associated with a 1.3-percentage-point increase in perceived job threat; the highest exposure quartile mentioned this worry three times as often as the lowest. The threat measure identifies respondents saying their own roles were already replaced or substantially reduced, or likely to experience these changes soon.
qs: One fifth of the respondents in our survey voiced concern about economic displacement.
For every 10-percentage-point increase in exposure, perceived job threat increased by 1.3 percentage points.
People in the top 25% of exposure mentioned the worry three times as often as those in the bottom 25%.
A respondent was coded as indicating job threat if they said their role was already being replaced or substantially reduced, or that such changes were likely in the near term (coded using Claude).

kp.k: Early-career respondents report greater displacement anxiety
kp.d: Career stage could be inferred for about half the sample, and early-career respondents were much more concerned about displacement than senior workers. Classification relied on contextual clues, including homework for early-career status and business ownership or hiring responsibilities for senior status. The authors connect this finding to their earlier tentative evidence of slower hiring of recent graduates and early-career US workers; the survey itself measures concern, not hiring outcomes.
qs: For about half of respondents in this survey, we were able to infer career stage from their answers.
We found that early-career respondents were much more likely to express concern about job displacement than senior workers.
For example, several users mentioned using Claude for homework, which put them in the early-career group.

kp.k: Self-reported productivity gains are substantial but incompletely observed
kp.d: Claude scored reported productivity effects on a deliberately non-centred 1–7 scale, ranging from less productive to transformatively more productive. The mean rating was 5.1, corresponding to substantially more productive; 3% reported negative or neutral effects, while 42% offered no clear productivity indication. These are classified testimonials rather than independently measured productivity outcomes, and the authors acknowledge likely positive selection among active users willing to participate.
qs: The mean productivity rating was 5.1, corresponding to “substantially more productive.”
Some 3% reported negative or neutral impacts, and 42% did not give a clear indication on productivity.
Our respondents were, of course, active Claude users who were willing to take a survey. This could make them more likely to report productivity benefits than the average user.

kp.k: Productivity benefits span high- and low-paid occupations
kp.d: High-paying occupations reported the largest gains, a pattern that persisted when computer and math occupations were excluded. Some of the lowest-paid workers also reported large gains, including through technical side projects rather than solely their existing jobs. Management occupations, mostly entrepreneurs building businesses, ranked highest, followed by computer and math; excluding solopreneurs left these groups tied. Wage comparisons used quartiles of BLS occupational median wages, not respondents’ individual incomes.
qs: This result is not driven only by coding; it holds when we leave out computer and math occupations.
Some of the lowest-paid workers describe high productivity gains as well.
One delivery driver, for example, was using Claude to start an e-commerce business, and a landscaper was building a music application.
Removing these “solopreneurs” still leaves management tied with computer and math occupations for showing the highest productivity benefit.

kp.k: Legal professions report comparatively mild productivity improvements
kp.d: Scientific and legal professions showed the mildest self-reported productivity improvements among major occupational groups. The authors report some lawyers’ concerns about AI following precise instructions, illustrated by a respondent describing repeated divergence from instructions for reading legal documents. This is survey evidence and a customer account carried by Anthropic, not a benchmark of legal accuracy or a finding that legal work cannot benefit from AI.
qs: The two groups exhibiting the mildest productivity improvements were workers in scientific and legal professions.
Some lawyers worried about AI’s ability to follow precise instructions.
I have given very specific rules about what is where, how to read a legal document, what I want it to do… but it diverges every time.

kp.k: Reported gains primarily accrue to users, with career differences
kp.d: About a quarter of interviews identified a beneficiary of productivity gains. Most of those respondents named themselves, through faster work, expanded scope or freed time; 10% named employers or clients asking for and receiving more work. In this beneficiary analysis, 60% of early-career workers indicated personal benefit versus 80% of senior professionals. The authors caution that enterprise users, absent from this personal-account survey, might report more value accruing to employers.
qs: Respondents indicated the recipient of these gains in about a quarter of interviews.
But 10% of respondents who named a recipient said that employers or clients were asking for and getting more work.
This depended on career stage: only 60% of early-career workers indicated that they personally benefited from AI, compared to 80% of senior professionals.
A more representative picture would also include enterprise users, who may be more likely to say the value accrues to their employers.

kp.k: Expanded scope exceeds speed as reported productivity mechanism
kp.d: The analysis distinguishes scope, speed, quality and cost benefits. Among users explicitly mentioning productivity effects, 48% cited scope expansion and 40% emphasised speed. Respondents described gaining new technical abilities and accelerating existing tasks; quality improvements often involved more thorough checking of code, contracts and paperwork, while a small share cited low cost. These categories describe reported experiences rather than measured improvements in legal quality.
qs: We find that the most common productivity enhancement is in scope, which was cited by 48% of users who explicitly mentioned productivity effects.
40% of users who mentioned productivity emphasized speed.
Quality gains often came from more thorough checks of code, contracts, and other paperwork.
I built a tool that helps me finish a financing task in 15 minutes that used to take 2 hours.

kp.k: Speedups and displacement fears exhibit a U-shaped relationship
kp.d: Using a separate inferred speed scale from 1 for much slower through 4 for unchanged to 7 for much faster, the authors find elevated perceived threat among both slowed-down users and those reporting the largest speedups. Some artists and writers found AI constraining in their own work while fearing its wider market effects. Among remaining respondents, threat increased with speedup. The proposed explanation—that rapidly shrinking task times create uncertainty about a role’s viability—is an interpretation, not demonstrated displacement.
qs: We found that the relationship between speedup and perceived job threat is U-shaped (see Figure 6).
For example, some creative workers, like fine artists and writers, found AI too stifling and rigid to help them at their own work.
For the remaining respondents, perceived job threat increases consistently with the level of speedup implied by their answers.
This makes some economic sense: if the time required to do one’s tasks is shrinking quickly, there may be more uncertainty about the future viability of the role.

kp.k: Individual accounts combine empowerment with intensified work demands
kp.d: Respondent accounts show productivity benefits coexisting with fears of replacement and harder work expectations. A software developer worried about replacement of junior positions; a market researcher acknowledged improved capability while fearing eventual substitution; another developer reported increasingly difficult assignments after AI arrived. These are qualitative examples, not estimates of the incidence of junior displacement or work intensification.
qs: the possibility of AI in its current state being used to replace junior positions.
In terms of improving my capability, it's no doubt. [B]ut in the future AI may replace my work.
when AI arrived, the project managers started giving harder and harder tickets and bugs to solve.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Massenkoff and Huang report that legal and scientific professionals described the mildest productivity improvements among occupational groups; an interviewed lawyer described difficulty getting AI to follow precise document-handling instructions.
pts.d: This is the source's principal legal-specific finding. It concerns inferred, self-reported productivity benefits, not measured legal performance or a prediction of lawyer replacement. The anonymous lawyer's account illustrates an instruction-following limitation experienced in legal-document work. The authors also report, across occupations, that quality gains often involved more thorough checks of contracts, code and other paperwork; they do not provide a separate legal quality measure.

pts.k: Across occupations, the authors find that greater observed exposure to Claude is associated with greater perceived job threat, and early-career respondents express more displacement concern than senior workers.
pts.d: One fifth of respondents voiced economic-displacement concerns. For the occupation-level job-threat measure, each 10-percentage-point increase in observed exposure was associated with a 1.3-percentage-point increase in perceived threat; the highest exposure quartile mentioned this concern three times as often as the lowest. These are findings about reported perceptions, not estimates of actual job losses. An interviewed software developer separately warned about replacement of junior positions. The authors refer to earlier research reporting tentative signs of slower US hiring of recent graduates and early-career workers, rather than establishing that slowdown with this survey.

pts.k: The authors report substantial perceived productivity benefits, especially through expanded capabilities and faster work, with high gains in both high- and low-paid occupations.
pts.d: The mean inferred productivity rating was 5.1 on the authors' seven-point scale, corresponding to 'substantially more productive.' High-paying occupations reported the largest gains, a relationship the authors say persists when computer and math occupations are excluded; some of the lowest-paid workers also reported large gains, sometimes on technical side projects rather than their main jobs. Management respondents, mostly entrepreneurs building businesses, ranked highest, followed by computer and math occupations. Among users explicitly mentioning productivity effects, 48% cited expanded scope and 40% emphasized speed. These findings describe reported experiences rather than experimentally measured output gains.

pts.k: Respondents generally identified themselves as beneficiaries of AI productivity gains, but some reported employers or clients obtaining more work; reported personal benefit was less common among early-career workers.
pts.d: Approximately one quarter of interviews identified a beneficiary. Within this subset, most respondents cited personal benefits such as faster tasks, broader scope and freed-up time, while 10% said employers or clients requested and received more work. The reported personal-benefit share was 60% for early-career workers versus 80% for senior professionals. An interviewed software developer described project managers assigning harder tasks after AI arrived. These are perceived destinations of gains, not measured distributions of economic surplus.

pts.k: The authors find a U-shaped association between reported speedup and perceived job threat: both users slowed by AI and those experiencing the largest speedups express elevated concern.
pts.d: Among respondents other than those reporting slowdown, perceived threat increased with inferred speedup. Some artists and writers described AI as stifling for their own work while fearing that its wider adoption would reduce their work opportunities. The authors suggest that rapidly shrinking task times may generate uncertainty about a role's future viability; this is an interpretation of the association, not a demonstrated causal mechanism or a forecast of displacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of an open-ended survey of approximately 81,000 personal-account Claude users, Claude-classified responses, occupational wage data and comparison with Anthropic's observed-exposure measure.
pts.d: The acknowledgements specify 80,508 participants. Claude-powered classifiers inferred occupations, career stage, sentiments and productivity benefits from responses. Career stage could be inferred for about half of respondents. Productivity was classified on a seven-point scale, and speedup on a separate seven-point scale. Occupational wage comparisons use BLS occupational median wages, not respondents' reported individual earnings. Observed exposure reflects the percentage of occupational tasks for which Claude is used. The source offers participant quotations as illustrative experience and references earlier Economic Index and labor-market research; it does not offer legal benchmarks, independently measured task performance or court cases as evidence for the legal-specific finding.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The April 22, 2026 report describes respondents' recent or current experiences and perceived displacement already occurring or likely in the near term; it supplies no fixed replacement timeline.
pts.d: The supplied text does not specify survey fieldwork dates. Findings are conditional on voluntary participation by personal-account Claude users and on what respondents spontaneously mentioned. The authors acknowledge possible selection bias, mistaken inference from contextual clues and a need for structured-survey confirmation. Some 42% gave no clear productivity indication, and 3% reported neutral or negative impacts. Personal-account sampling may particularly overstate the share of benefits flowing to users rather than employers; enterprise users might report a different distribution.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source addresses workers across occupations and career stages, entrepreneurs, employers and clients; its legal-specific coverage concerns professionals' productivity and instruction-following difficulties.
pts.d: Legal and scientific workers report comparatively mild improvements; managers and entrepreneurs, software developers and some low-paid workers report larger gains. Early-career respondents express greater displacement anxiety and less frequent personal benefit than senior professionals. Highly exposed occupations such as software engineering express more concern than less-exposed occupations such as elementary teaching. Creative workers may fear lost opportunities even when AI is unhelpful in their own work. Employers and clients sometimes receive more output. The source does not distinguish law-firm types, in-house legal departments, ALSPs or legal client segments, and makes no specific claim about legal pricing, staffing structures or access to justice.
